extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and anyone learning principles of induction and probability
extracted.subtask_description: General principles for forming and evaluating inductive inferences, approximate generalizations, reasoning from probabilities, and the treatment of resemblance, existence, and mathematical truths in scientific argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply general averages only to average cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A general average should only be applied to cases which are neither known, nor can be presumed, to be other than average cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Averages (e.g. 'nine out of every ten A are B') are useful only when nothing else is known about the particular instance; they are commonly of little use for individual cases that differ from the class mean. Example: life tables inform insurers about large populations but not the chance for any particular life, which may be better or worse than the average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply whole-genus averages to known species/subclasses
rubrics_metrics.description: If we know, of any particular instance i, not only that it falls under A, but to what species or variety of A it belongs, we shall generally err in applying to i the average struck for the whole genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subclass/species-level information is available, use the average for that subclass rather than the genus-level average; genus averages may mislead if the species differs materially in the relevant proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of joining approximate generalizations: Addition vs Deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a judgment is grounded on two approximate generalizations taken in conjunction, they may cooperate in two ways: (1) Addition — each proposition separately applies to the case, yielding a higher joint probability (self-corroborative); (2) Deduction — one proposition applies only by virtue of the other, yielding a lower probability than either (self-infirmative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Addition — 'Most A are B; most C are B; this thing is both A and C; therefore probably B' (analogous to testimony of two independent witnesses). Deduction — 'Most A are B; most C are A; this is C; therefore probably A, so probably B' (a hearsay-of-hearsay type of reasoning). Longer chains of the deduction type reduce probability at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute joint probabilities only under independence; otherwise beware
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct evaluation of chances when combining generalizations presupposes that the probabilities arising from each generalization are independent of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A and C are independent regarding B, the chance that a thing which is both A and C is not-B can be computed as the product of the separate non-B probabilities (example and corrected arithmetic shown leading to six-to-one odds in a two-witness case). If A and C are connected (dependence), the joint probability may be no greater than from one alone; dependence can make not-B cases overlap and invalidate multiplicative combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: When joining approximate generalizations by deduction, probability diminishes multiplicatively
rubrics_metrics.description: From successive premises of the form 'Most A are B', 'Most B are C', etc., the probability that a given A is ultimately D diminishes at each inferred step; the error of the conclusion aggregates from the errors of the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical illustration: if Most A are B is 9/10 and Most B are C is 8/9, then the proportion of A that are C is 8/10; adding another step multiplies by that step's proportion (e.g., 7/8 -> 7/10). Because empirical generalizations rarely admit exact numerical estimation, the useful rule is to remember that probability decreases with each illation and that chains of presumptive evidence beyond a few removes are worthless unless premises are nearly universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform certain approximate generalizations into universal propositions with explicit provisos
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reason for calling a generalization approximate is only the inconvenience of going further, and we know the distinguishing character of exceptions, we may substitute an universal proposition with a proviso recording the exceptional conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By expressing each approximate premise as a universal statement conditioned on explicit hypotheses, the resulting conclusion can be treated as universal subject to the recorded provisos; the aggregate of provisos at the end indicates how far the conclusion is from universal truth. Example: 'Most persons with uncontrolled power employ it ill' -> 'All persons who have uncontrolled power employ it ill, provided they are not persons of unusual strength of judgment and rectitude of purpose.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate propositions can be treated as effectively universal for inquiries about multitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiries concerning the properties of masses (e.g., political science, statecraft) often only require knowing what 'most' persons do, because the actions of the mass determine collective results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical and long-term arrangements affecting communities, approximate generalizations about human nature are often as suitable as universal laws and suffice for scientific reasoning about populations; what is true approximately of individuals can be true absolutely of masses. This justifies the scientific character of social inquiry despite reliance on probable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a phenomenon can be established by a single observed instance
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions that affirm bare existence are sufficiently proved by a single instance; 'That ghosts exist' would be established if even once they were positively ascertained to have been seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence claims (of phenomena) are not the province of metaphysics here but of inductive logic applied to phenomena; once an occurrence has been observed, it establishes the possibility and hence the existence in the inductive sense, subject to conditions under which it happens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer existence from inductive laws of succession or coexistence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phenomenon is not directly perceived, its existence is inferred from other phenomena ascertained by induction to be connected with it by succession or coexistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We prove the existence of a thing by proving it is connected with some known thing via observed uniformities; belief in absent phenomena (e.g., Emperor of China, distant stars) is a conviction that under suitable conditions they would be perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine resemblances by comparing through a third object when direct comparison is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: When two objects cannot be brought into direct juxtaposition or minutely compared, comparison is made by means of a third object (e.g., a standard) that can be transported between them; this is the scientific process for ascertaining resemblances and differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing two straight lines via a foot rule; mathematical axioms ('things equal to the same thing are equal to one another') underpin indirect comparison. Many apparent resemblances require minute part-by-part comparison; inference from other, more accessible resemblances is needed when direct inspection is impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical laws of resemblance differ from empirical laws of resemblance and are independent of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of equality, inequality, and proportionality (mathematics) are uniformities not derived from causes and are valid irrespective of the origin of phenomena; they are the only laws of resemblance that can be treated independently of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical resemblances (e.g., angle of reflection equals angle of incidence) are tied to causal laws, whereas mathematical equalities (e.g., opposite angles equal) hold universally. The elementary axioms of mathematics are inductive truths grounded in repeated perception and simple observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical definitions connote modes of formation; arithmetical propositions state modes of formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Number words denote physical aggregates and connote the characteristic manner in which an aggregate is formed and may be separated into parts; arithmetical propositions assert that certain aggregates can be formed from others in particular ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Saying '12' denotes dozens of things and implies specific modes of forming 12 (e.g., 12 = 10 + 2 or 6 + 6); the cube of 12 = 1728 is a claim about forming aggregates of aggregates. This grounds arithmetic in observable composition and decomposition of collections.
